---
title: "Interpreting a logistic regression"
---

## Packages

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)
```

## A sore throat after surgery

`licorice_gargle` (from `medicaldata`) is a trial of 235 adults
having thoracic surgery with a large breathing tube.
Before the tube went in,
they were randomized to gargle licorice or sugar water.
Our outcome is any sore throat 30 minutes after surgery.

## Recode the variables

```{r}
sore <- licorice_gargle |>
  mutate(
    sore_throat = factor(pacu30min_throatPain > 0,
                         levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                         labels = c("no", "yes")),
    treatment = factor(treat, levels = c(0, 1),
                       labels = c("sugar", "licorice")),
    smoking = factor(preOp_smoking, levels = c(3, 2, 1),
                     labels = c("never", "past",
                                "current"))
  ) |>
  select(sore_throat, treatment,
         bmi = preOp_calcBMI, smoking) |>
  drop_na()
```

## Which level are we modelling?

- `logistic_reg()` models the odds of the outcome's **second** level
- `sore_throat` has the levels `no`, then `yes`,
  so every result is about the odds of a sore throat
- The predictors are a mix of both kinds:
  - `treatment`: 2 levels, so 1 dummy variable (reference `sugar`)
  - `bmi`: continuous, in kg/m²
  - `smoking`: 3 levels, so 2 dummy variables (reference `never`)

```{r}
count(sore, sore_throat)
```

## Fit the model

```{r}
sore_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  fit(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
      data = sore)

tidy(sore_fit, conf.int = TRUE)
```

- These estimates are on the **log-odds** scale,
  $\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right)$,
  which is hard to read

## Exponentiate to get odds ratios

```{r}
sore_or <- sore_fit |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
sore_or
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# pull one number out of the odds ratio table, for the sentences on the next slides
get_or <- function(term, column = "estimate") {
  sore_or[[column]][sore_or$term == term]
}
# show an odds ratio with 2 decimals, and turn it into a percent lower
two <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
pct_lower <- function(term) round(100 * (1 - get_or(term)))
```

- `exponentiate = TRUE` turns each estimate and its interval
  into an **odds ratio**
  (`std.error`, `statistic`, and `p.value` stay on the log-odds scale)
- An odds ratio of 1 means no difference,
  below 1 means lower odds,
  and above 1 means higher odds

## Interpreting a continuous variable

> For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable],
> we expect the odds of [outcome] to be multiplied by [odds ratio],
> all else remaining the same.

For `bmi`:

> For every 1 kg/m² increase in BMI,
> we expect the odds of a sore throat to be multiplied by `r two(get_or("bmi"))`,
> all else remaining the same
> (95% CI: `r two(get_or("bmi", "conf.low"))` to `r two(get_or("bmi", "conf.high"))`).

- Multiplied by `r two(get_or("bmi"))` is the same as
  `r pct_lower("bmi")`% lower odds
- The interval includes 1,
  so the data don't show a clear effect of BMI

## Interpreting a categorical variable

> We expect the odds of [outcome] for [level]
> to be [odds ratio] times the odds for [reference level],
> all else remaining the same.

For `treatmentlicorice`:

> We expect the odds of a sore throat for patients who gargled licorice
> to be `r two(get_or("treatmentlicorice"))` times the odds
> for patients who gargled sugar water,
> all else remaining the same
> (95% CI: `r two(get_or("treatmentlicorice", "conf.low"))` to `r two(get_or("treatmentlicorice", "conf.high"))`).

- That's `r pct_lower("treatmentlicorice")`% lower odds,
  and the interval doesn't include 1

## A categorical variable with more levels

Each dummy variable compares one level with the reference, `never`.
For `smokingpast`:

> We expect the odds of a sore throat for past smokers
> to be `r two(get_or("smokingpast"))` times the odds for people who never smoked,
> all else remaining the same
> (95% CI: `r two(get_or("smokingpast", "conf.low"))` to `r two(get_or("smokingpast", "conf.high"))`).

- `smokingcurrent` compares current smokers with people who never smoked,
  not with past smokers
- Its interval (`r two(get_or("smokingcurrent", "conf.low"))` to `r two(get_or("smokingcurrent", "conf.high"))`)
  includes 1, so that comparison isn't clear

## Odds, not probability

- An odds ratio compares odds, not probabilities
- Say "`r two(get_or("treatmentlicorice"))` times the odds",
  not "`r two(get_or("treatmentlicorice"))` times as likely"
  or "`r pct_lower("treatmentlicorice")`% less likely"
- The two are close only when the outcome is rare,
  and here `r round(100 * mean(sore$sore_throat == "yes"))`% of patients had a sore throat

## The same model in base R

Base R's `glm()` fits the same model with less code:

```{r}
glm(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
    family = binomial, data = sore) |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
```

- `family = binomial` is what makes `glm()` a logistic regression
- The same odds ratios and intervals as `logistic_reg()`
- We use tidymodels because every kind of model goes through the same steps
